UNITS.title: Computational Thinking

lesson.p: Before writing code, programmers think through the problem. There are four big skills:
list: <mark>Decomposition</mark>: break a big problem into smaller parts.
<mark>Pattern recognition</mark>: notice what repeats or is similar.
<mark>Abstraction</mark>: ignore details that don't matter right now.
<mark>Algorithm</mark>: write clear step-by-step instructions that always finish.

lesson.p: <mark>Pseudocode</mark> describes an algorithm in plain, code-like English. It isn't a real language, so anyone can read it. Here's an algorithm to find the average of test scores:

code.all:
SET total TO 0
FOR EACH score IN scores
    ADD score TO total
END FOR
SET average TO total / COUNT(scores)
DISPLAY average

lesson.p: A <mark>flowchart</mark> draws an algorithm with shapes:
list: Oval: start or end
Rectangle: a process (do something)
Diamond: a decision (yes/no question)
Parallelogram: input or output

lesson.p: Every program is built from three structures: <mark>sequence</mark> (steps in order), <mark>selection</mark> (choosing with if), and <mark>iteration</mark> (repeating with loops). You'll learn each one in this course.

terms: Breaking a problem into smaller, manageable parts
Hiding details that aren't needed to solve the problem
A precise, step-by-step set of instructions that finishes
Plain-language description of an algorithm's steps
Diagram of an algorithm using shapes and arrows
Steps run one after another, in order
Choosing a path based on a condition (if)

qs.q: Planning a school dance by splitting it into music, food, and decorations is an example of:
qs.e: Splitting a big job into smaller parts is decomposition.

qs.q: In a flowchart, what does a diamond shape mean?
qs.e: Diamonds ask a yes/no question and branch.

qs.q: A traffic simulation treats every car as a moving dot and ignores color and brand. This is:
qs.e: Abstraction removes details that don't matter for the problem.

qs.q: Which are the three basic control structures?
qs.e: Every algorithm can be built from sequence, selection, and iteration.

qs.q: Which is the best example of an algorithm?
c: "Do some math until it feels right."
"Add the two numbers, divide by 2, display the result."
qs.e: An algorithm has clear, precise steps that end.

qs.q: In a flowchart, the parallelogram shape represents:
qs.e: Parallelograms are used for input (get data) and output (show data).

qs.q: To draw a square you notice "move forward, turn right" happens 4 times. Noticing this is:
qs.e: Spotting a repeated step is pattern recognition, and it hints you can use a loop.

qs.q: Why do programmers write pseudocode before coding?
c: To plan the logic without worrying about syntax
qs.e: Pseudocode lets you focus on the steps first, then translate them into a real language.

UNITS.title: How Computers Store Data
UNITS.blurb: Bits, bytes, binary, hex, and characters.

lesson.p: Computers store everything as <mark>bits</mark>: 0 or 1 (off or on). A group of 8 bits is a <mark>byte</mark>. With n bits you can make 2ⁿ different patterns, so one byte holds 2⁸ = 256 values (0 to 255).
In <mark>binary</mark>, each place is worth double the place to its right. Add the place values where there's a 1.
Find the biggest place value that fits, write a 1, subtract, and repeat. For 13: 8 fits (13 − 8 = 5), 4 fits (5 − 4 = 1), 2 doesn't, 1 fits. So 13 = 1101.

<mark>Hexadecimal</mark> uses digits 0–9 and A–F (A = 10 … F = 15). Each hex digit stands for 4 bits, so it's a short way to write binary. Colors on the web use hex, like #FF0000 for red. Example: 2F = 2 × 16 + 15 = 47.
Text is stored as numbers too. <mark>ASCII</mark> gives each English character a number ('A' = 65, 'a' = 97). <mark>Unicode</mark> extends this to every language and emoji.

terms: Base-2 number system using only 0 and 1
Character code that maps English characters to numbers (A = 65)
Character standard covering all languages and emoji
How much a digit is worth based on its position

qs.q: What is binary 1011 in decimal?
What is decimal 13 in binary?
How many different values can 8 bits represent?
qs.e: 2⁸ = 256 values (0 through 255).

qs.q: What is the largest number you can store in 4 bits?
What is hexadecimal 1F in decimal?
One byte is made of how many bits?
qs.e: A byte is 8 bits.

qs.q: What is ASCII used for?
qs.e: ASCII maps characters to numbers so text can be stored in binary.

qs.q: Why was Unicode created when ASCII already existed?
c: ASCII couldn't represent most of the world's languages and symbols
Unicode uses fewer bits for every character
qs.e: ASCII covers English characters. Unicode covers every writing system and emoji.

qs.q: What is binary 100000 in decimal?
qs.e: The 1 is in the 32s place.

UNITS.title: Variables, Types & Input
UNITS.blurb: Store data and talk to the user.

lesson.p: A <mark>variable</mark> is a named box that stores a value. You can change what's inside later. The <mark>data type</mark> says what kind of value it is.
list: int: whole numbers like 16
float (Python) / double (Java): decimals like 3.8
string: text in quotes like "Ava"
boolean: True/False (Python) or true/false (Java)

lesson.p: Python figures out the type for you. Java makes you write the type first.

code.py:
name = "Ava"
age = 16
gpa = 3.8
is_senior = False
print(name, "is", age)     # Ava is 16

lesson.p: Programs can ask the user for data.

code.py:
name = input("Your name? ")        # always a string
age = int(input("Your age? "))     # convert to int
print("Hi", name)

after.py: In Python, input() always gives you a string. Use int() or float() to turn it into a number.
after.java: In Java, use a Scanner. nextLine() reads text, nextInt() reads a whole number, nextDouble() reads a decimal.

lesson.p: Names can't start with a digit, can't have spaces, and can't be keywords like class. Pick names that explain the value: total_score in Python or totalScore in Java (camelCase).

terms: A named storage location for a value
The kind of value: int, float/double, string, boolean
A whole number with no decimal
A number with a decimal point
A value that is only true or false
Storing a value in a variable with =
A value that shouldn't change once set

qs.q: Which data type is best for the number of students in a class?
qs.e: A count is a whole number, so int.

qs.q: Which of these is a boolean value?

e.py: True (capital T, no quotes) is a boolean. "True" in quotes is a string.
e.java: true (lowercase, no quotes) is a boolean. "true" in quotes is a String.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
x = 5
y = x
x = 9
print(y)

qs.e: y got a copy of 5. Changing x later doesn't change y.

qs.q: Which is a valid, well-chosen variable name?
qs.e: Names can't start with a digit, contain spaces, or be keywords like class.

q.py: What type of value does input() always return?
q.java: Which Scanner method reads a whole line of text?

e.py: input() always returns a string. Wrap it in int() or float() to get a number.
e.java: nextLine() reads everything up to the Enter key.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.java: System.out.println("5" + "3");

qs.e: Both are strings, so + joins them: "53".

qs.q: What is the value of x at the end?

q.py: By convention, how do Python programmers name a constant?
q.java: Which Java keyword stops a variable's value from being changed?

e.py: Python has no constant keyword. ALL_CAPS signals "don't change this".
e.java: final makes a variable a constant: final int MAX_SCORE = 100;

qs.q: Which type would you use to store a student's GPA, like 3.75?

e.py: Decimals are floats in Python.
e.java: Decimals are usually doubles in Java.

UNITS.title: Operators & Expressions
UNITS.blurb: Math, division rules, and order of operations.

lesson.p: + - * / work like math class. Two more matter a lot in CS: modulus % gives the remainder, and integer division keeps only the whole part.

code.py:
print(17 / 5)    # 3.4  (/ always gives a decimal)
print(17 // 5)   # 3    (floor division)
print(17 % 5)    # 2    (remainder)
print(2 ** 3)    # 8    (exponent)
code.java:
System.out.println(17 / 5);     // 3   (int / int drops the decimal)
System.out.println(17.0 / 5);   // 3.4
System.out.println(17 % 5);     // 2   (remainder)
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 3));  // 8.0

lesson.p: Just like PEMDAS: parentheses first, then exponents, then * / // % from left to right, then + and −. So 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, but (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.
n % 2 == 0 checks if n is even. n % 10 gives the last digit. minutes % 60 gives leftover minutes after hours.
Compound assignment like x += 3 means x = x + 3. To change a type, convert (or cast) it.

code.py:
x = 4
x *= 3         # 12
print(int(9.99))    # 9  (drops the decimal)
print(float(7))     # 7.0
print(str(95))      # "95"
code.java:
int x = 4;
x *= 3;        // 12
System.out.println((int) 9.99);   // 9  (drops the decimal)
System.out.println((double) 7);   // 7.0
x++;           // adds 1

terms: Division that keeps only the whole-number part
The order operators are evaluated (like PEMDAS)
A combination of values and operators that produces a value
Shortcut like x += 3 for x = x + 3
Changing a value from one type to another

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(17 // 5)
code.java: System.out.println(17 / 5);

e.py: // is floor division: 17 // 5 = 3.
e.java: Both are ints, so Java drops the decimal: 3.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(7 / 2)
code.java: System.out.println(7 / 2);

e.py: In Python, / always gives a decimal: 3.5.
e.java: int / int in Java gives an int: 3. Use 7.0 / 2 to get 3.5.

qs.q: What is 17 % 5?
qs.e: 17 = 5 × 3 + 2. The remainder is 2.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(2 + 3 * 4)
code.java: System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);

qs.e: Multiply first: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.java: System.out.println(10 - 4 / 2);

qs.q: Which condition is true only when n is even?
qs.e: Even numbers leave remainder 0 when divided by 2.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(int(9.99))
code.java: System.out.println((int) 9.99);

qs.e: Converting to int chops off the decimal. It does not round.

qs.q: What is x at the end?
What is printed?

code.py: print(2 ** 3)
code.java: System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 3));

e.py: ** is the exponent operator: 2³ = 8.
e.java: Math.pow always returns a double, so it prints 8.0.

qs.q: What is 125 % 10?
qs.e: % 10 gives the last digit of a whole number: 5.

UNITS.title: Strings

lesson.p: A string is a sequence of characters. Each character has an index that starts at 0, not 1.
These are the moves you'll use most:

code.py:
word = "TEXAS"
print(len(word))       # 5
print(word[0])         # T
print(word[1:3])       # EX   (stops before index 3)
print(word.lower())    # texas
print(word.find("A"))  # 3
print("ha" * 3)        # hahaha
code.java:
String word = "TEXAS";
System.out.println(word.length());        // 5
System.out.println(word.charAt(0));       // T
System.out.println(word.substring(1, 3)); // EX  (stops before index 3)
System.out.println(word.toLowerCase());   // texas
System.out.println(word.indexOf("A"));    // 3
System.out.println("ha".repeat(3));       // hahaha

p.py: In word[a:b], a is included and b is not. The slice has b − a characters. word[-1] is the last character.
p.java: In substring(a, b), a is included and b is not. The result has b − a characters. The last character is word.charAt(word.length() - 1).

p.py: You can't add a string and a number: "Score: " + 95 is an error. Use "Score: " + str(95). Compare text with ==.
p.java: Java turns numbers into text when you add them to a String: "Score: " + 95 works. But compare text with .equals(), not ==.

terms: The position of a character, starting at 0
Number of characters in a string
A piece of a string from one index up to (not including) another
Can't be changed in place; string methods return a new string

qs.q: In word = "TEXAS", what index is the first character?
qs.e: Indexes start at 0.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
word = "TEXAS"
print(word[4])
code.java:
String word = "TEXAS";
System.out.println(word.charAt(4));

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
word = "TEXAS"
print(word[1:4])
code.java:
String word = "TEXAS";
System.out.println(word.substring(1, 4));

qs.e: Indexes 1, 2, 3 (stops before 4): E X A.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(len("TEXAS"))
code.java: System.out.println("TEXAS".length());

qs.e: There are 5 characters. The last index is 4, but the length is 5.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
word = "TEXAS"
print(word.find("A"))
code.java:
String word = "TEXAS";
System.out.println(word.indexOf("A"));

qs.e: The first A is at index 3. If it weren't found, you'd get -1.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print("Score: " + 95)
code.java: System.out.println("Score: " + 95);

e.py: Python won't add a str and an int. You'd need str(95). (A comma in print also works.)
e.java: Java converts 95 to text when you add it to a String: Score: 95.

qs.q: How do you check whether two strings s1 and s2 have the same text?

e.py: In Python, == compares the text.
e.java: In Java, == checks if they're the same object. Use .equals() to compare the text.

qs.q: What happens?

code.py:
word = "TEXAS"
print(word[5])
code.java:
String word = "TEXAS";
System.out.println(word.charAt(5));

e.py: The last index is 4, so word[5] raises IndexError.
e.java: The last index is 4, so charAt(5) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

qs.q: Which gets the LAST character of word, whatever its length?

e.py: Negative indexes count from the end: word[-1] is the last character.
e.java: The last index is length − 1.

UNITS.title: Making Decisions

lesson.p: Conditions compare values and give a boolean: == equal, != not equal, < > <= >=. Don't mix up = (store a value) and == (compare).
<mark>Selection</mark> lets a program choose. Only the first true branch runs.

after.py: Python uses a colon and indentation to show what's inside each branch.
after.java: Java uses parentheses around the condition and braces { } around each branch.

lesson.p: Combine conditions with <mark>and</mark>, <mark>or</mark>, and <mark>not</mark>.

code.py:
age = 15
print(age >= 13 and age <= 19)   # True  (both must be true)
print(age < 5 or age > 65)       # False (at least one must be true)
print(not True)                  # False
code.java:
int age = 15;
System.out.println(age >= 13 && age <= 19);  // true  (both)
System.out.println(age < 5 || age > 65);     // false (at least one)
System.out.println(!true);                   // false

lesson.p: Check the most specific (or highest) condition first. If you test score >= 70 before score >= 90, a 95 gets a C because the first true branch wins.

terms: An expression that is true or false
Choosing which code runs using if/else
True only if both sides are true
True if at least one side is true
Flips true to false and false to true
An if statement inside another if

qs.q: What is printed when score is 85?
qs.e: 85 >= 80 is the first true condition, so only B prints.

qs.q: If x is 7, what is the value of this expression?

code.py: x > 5 and x < 10

qs.e: 7 > 5 is true and 7 < 10 is true, so both are true.

qs.q: What is the value of this expression?
qs.e: 3 > 1 is true, and not flips it to false.

qs.q: What's the difference between = and ==?
c: = assigns a value; == compares two values
qs.e: x = 5 stores 5. x == 5 asks "is x equal to 5?"

qs.q: What is printed when temp is 90? (Look closely: there are two separate ifs.)
qs.e: These are two separate if statements, so both are checked. 90 > 80 prints hot, and 90 > 40 prints mild.

qs.q: For which ages is this true?

code.py: age >= 13 and age <= 19

qs.e: Both ends are included because of >= and <=.

qs.q: When is (a or b) true?

code.py: a or b
code.java: a || b

c: When at least one is true
qs.e: or is true if either side, or both, is true.

qs.q: A student wrote this grader, and a score of 95 prints C. Why?
c: The first true branch runs, and >= 70 is checked first
qs.e: Only the first true branch runs. Put the highest cutoff (90) first.

UNITS.title: Loops

lesson.p: <mark>Iteration</mark> repeats code so you don't copy and paste it. Use a <mark>for loop</mark> when you know how many times to repeat, and a <mark>while loop</mark> when you repeat until something changes.
Count from a start value up to (not including) a stop value.

code.py:
for i in range(5):         # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
    print(i)

for i in range(2, 10, 2):  # 2, 4, 6, 8   (start, stop, step)
    print(i)

for i in range(5, 0, -1):  # 5, 4, 3, 2, 1
    print(i)

lesson.p: A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true. Something inside must change, or you get an <mark>infinite loop</mark>.

code.py:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1          # without this line, it never stops
print("Liftoff!")

lesson.p: To add things up, start a total at 0 before the loop and add to it inside the loop.

code.py:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
print(total)     # 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10

lesson.p: A loop inside a loop runs the inner loop completely for every pass of the outer loop. 3 outer passes × 2 inner passes = 6 runs. break exits a loop immediately.

terms: Repeats a set number of times (count-controlled)
Repeats while a condition is true (condition-controlled)
A loop whose condition never becomes false
A variable that builds up a total inside a loop

qs.q: What is the LAST number printed?

code.py:
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

qs.e: It counts 0 to 4. It stops before 5.

qs.q: How many times does the loop run?

code.py:
for i in range(2, 10, 2):
    print(i)

qs.e: i is 2, 4, 6, 8. Four times.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i
print(total)

qs.e: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The loop stops before 5.

qs.q: What is n after the loop ends?
qs.e: 10 → 7 → 4 → 1 → -2. Now n > 0 is false, so the loop stops.

qs.q: What usually causes an infinite while loop?
c: Forgetting to change the variable in the condition
qs.e: If nothing inside the loop changes the condition, it stays true forever.

qs.q: How many stars are printed?
qs.e: The inner loop runs 2 times for each of 3 outer passes: 3 × 2 = 6.

qs.q: You want to keep asking for a password until the user types the right one. Which loop fits best?
qs.e: You don't know how many tries it will take, so use a condition-controlled while loop.

qs.q: How many numbers are printed?
qs.e: It prints 0, 1, 2, 3, then break stops the loop when i is 4.

qs.q: Which loop prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1?

e.py: Start at 5, stop before 0, step -1. range(5, 0) with no step is empty.
e.java: Start at 5, keep going while i > 0, and subtract 1 each time.

UNITS.title: Functions & Methods
UNITS.blurb: Reuse code with parameters and return values.

lesson.p: A <mark>function</mark> (called a <mark>method</mark> in Java) is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. It helps you decompose a problem and avoid repeating code.
Parameters are the inputs listed in the definition. Arguments are the actual values you pass in when you call it. return sends a value back.

code.py:
def area(width, height):     # width, height are parameters
    return width * height

result = area(3, 4)          # 3 and 4 are arguments
print(result)                # 12

after.py: A function with no return statement gives back None.
after.java: The word before the name is the return type. A method that returns nothing has return type void.

lesson.p: As soon as return runs, the function stops. Any lines after it in the same block never run.
A variable created inside a function only exists inside that function. This is its <mark>scope</mark>. Trying to use it outside causes an error.

terms: A named, reusable block of code
A variable in the function definition that receives input
The actual value passed in when the function is called
The value a function sends back to the caller
Means the function returns no value
Where in the program a variable can be used
Running a function by using its name with parentheses

qs.q: What is printed?
qs.e: The inner call gives 6. Then twice(6) gives 12.

qs.q: In area(3, 4), what are 3 and 4 called?
qs.e: Values passed in a call are arguments. The names in the definition are parameters.

q.py: What does a Python function return if it has no return statement?
q.java: What is the return type of a Java method that returns nothing?

e.py: With no return, a Python function gives back None.
e.java: void means the method doesn't return a value.

qs.q: What happens?

code.py:
def setup():
    secret = 42

setup()
print(secret)

c: An error, because secret only exists inside setup
qs.e: secret's scope is the function. Outside it, the variable doesn't exist.

qs.q: What is the main reason to write functions?
c: To reuse code and break problems into smaller parts
Because every line must be in a function
qs.e: Functions support decomposition and stop you from repeating code.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
def greet(name):
    return "Hi " + name

msg = greet("Lee")
print(msg + "!")

qs.e: greet gives back "Hi Lee", and then "!" is added.

qs.q: What is printed when check(10) is called?
qs.e: return "big" runs and ends the function immediately.

qs.q: area needs two arguments. What happens with area(5)?
c: It uses 0 for the missing one
An error: the call is missing an argument
qs.e: The number of arguments must match the parameters.

UNITS.title: Lists & Arrays
UNITS.blurb: Store many values and loop through them.

p.py: A list stores many values in order. Each item has an index starting at 0. Lists can grow with append.
p.java: An array stores many values of the same type in order. Each item has an index starting at 0. Arrays have a fixed size. Use an ArrayList when you need it to grow.

code.py:
scores = [88, 92, 75, 100]
print(scores[0])      # 88
print(len(scores))    # 4
print(scores[-1])     # 100 (last item)
scores.append(67)     # now 5 items
scores[1] = 95        # change an item
code.java:
int[] scores = {88, 92, 75, 100};
System.out.println(scores[0]);       // 88
System.out.println(scores.length);   // 4
System.out.println(scores[scores.length - 1]);  // 100 (last)
scores[1] = 95;                      // change an item

lesson.p: Looping through every item is called <mark>traversing</mark>. Use an index loop when you need positions, or a for-each loop when you just need the values.

code.py:
for s in scores:                 # for-each
    print(s)

for i in range(len(scores)):     # by index
    print(i, scores[i])

lesson.p: Find the maximum: start with the first item, then replace it whenever you find something bigger.
A list of 4 items has indexes 0 to 3. Asking for index 4 crashes the program with an <mark>index out of bounds</mark> error.

terms: An ordered collection of values under one name
One value stored in a list or array
Visit every element, usually with a loop
Using an index that doesn't exist
How to add items to a growable list

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
scores = [88, 92, 75, 100]
print(scores[2])
code.java:
int[] scores = {88, 92, 75, 100};
System.out.println(scores[2]);

qs.e: Index 0 is 88, 1 is 92, 2 is 75.

qs.q: A list or array has 4 elements. What is the index of the last one?
qs.e: Indexes run from 0 to length − 1.

qs.q: What happens?

code.py:
scores = [88, 92, 75, 100]
print(scores[4])
code.java:
int[] scores = {88, 92, 75, 100};
System.out.println(scores[4]);

c: An index out of range error

e.py: Index 4 doesn't exist, so you get IndexError.
e.java: Index 4 doesn't exist, so you get ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

qs.q: What is printed?
qs.e: Only 9 and 7 are greater than 5.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
nums = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
for i in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[i]
print(total)

q.py: What is len(nums) after this code?
q.java: An int[] has length 4. Can you add a 5th element to it?

code.py:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.append(4)

java: No. Arrays have a fixed size, so you'd use an ArrayList

e.py: append adds one item to the end, so there are now 4.
e.java: Arrays can't grow. An ArrayList can, with list.add(5).

qs.q: Which expression gets the LAST element of nums, whatever its length?

e.py: nums[-1] counts from the end.
e.java: The last index is length − 1. Java doesn't allow negative indexes.

qs.q: What does nums contain after this runs?
qs.e: The loop changes every element by its index.

UNITS.title: Searching & Sorting

lesson.p: <mark>Linear search</mark> checks each item one by one until it finds the target. It works on any list, but a list of 1,000 items might take 1,000 checks.

Binary search only works on a sorted list. Check the middle item. If the target is smaller, throw away the right half; if bigger, the left half. Each step cuts the list in half, so 1,000 items takes about 10 checks.

list: <mark>Selection sort</mark>: find the smallest item and swap it to the front. Repeat for the rest.
<mark>Bubble sort</mark>: compare neighbors and swap if they're out of order. The biggest item "bubbles" to the end each pass.
<mark>Insertion sort</mark>: take each item and slide it into its place in the sorted part on the left, like sorting cards in your hand.
lesson.p: Three sorts you should know:
Sorting [5, 2, 9, 1] from smallest to biggest:

code.all:
Selection, pass 1:  smallest is 1, swap with 5  →  [1, 2, 9, 5]
Bubble, pass 1:     5↔2, 5 and 9 ok, 9↔1      →  [2, 5, 1, 9]

terms: Check every item in order until the target is found
Repeatedly check the middle of a sorted list and discard half
Repeatedly select the smallest item and swap it into place
Swap neighboring items that are out of order; repeat
Insert each item into its place in the sorted section
How the work grows as the data gets bigger

qs.q: What must be true about a list before you can use binary search?
c: It has an even number of items
qs.e: Binary search depends on order to know which half to throw away.

qs.q: Worst case, how many items does linear search check in a list of 100?
qs.e: If the target is last (or missing), it checks all 100.

qs.q: About how many checks does binary search need for 1,000 sorted items?
qs.e: Halving 1,000 about 10 times gets you to 1 item.

qs.q: After ONE pass of selection sort (smallest to biggest), what is [5, 2, 9, 1]?
qs.e: Selection sort swaps the smallest (1) into the front.

qs.q: After ONE pass of bubble sort (smallest to biggest), what is [5, 2, 9, 1]?
qs.e: Swap 5 and 2, leave 5 and 9, swap 9 and 1. The biggest ends up last.

qs.q: Using the find function from the lesson, what does find([4, 9, 2, 7], 7) return?
qs.e: 7 is at index 3.

qs.q: Using the same find function, what does find([4, 9, 2, 7], 5) return?
qs.e: 5 isn't in the list, so the loop finishes and returns -1.

qs.q: Binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]. Which item is checked FIRST? (middle index = (0 + 9) / 2, rounded down)
qs.e: Middle index is 4, which holds 16. 23 is bigger, so search the right half.

qs.q: Which sort works like sorting cards in your hand, sliding each new card into place?
qs.e: Insertion sort builds a sorted section by inserting one item at a time.

UNITS.title: Objects & Classes
UNITS.blurb: Model real things with your own types.

lesson.p: A <mark>class</mark> is a blueprint. An <mark>object</mark> is one thing built from that blueprint. A class lists the data each object has (<mark>attributes</mark> or fields) and what it can do (<mark>methods</mark>).
The <mark>constructor</mark> runs when you create an object and sets its starting values.

code.py:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):    # constructor
        self.name = name         # attribute
        self.tricks = 0

    def learn(self):             # method
        self.tricks += 1

rex = Dog("Rex")      # create an object
rex.learn()
print(rex.name, rex.tricks)    # Rex 1

p.py: self means "this particular object." It lets each Dog keep its own name and tricks.
p.java: this means "this particular object." It tells apart the field this.name from the parameter name.

lesson.p: Encapsulation keeps an object's data protected and changes it only through methods. In Java, fields are private and you use getters and setters. In Python, a leading underscore like _name signals "don't touch directly."

terms: A blueprint that defines attributes and methods
One specific thing created from a class
A function that belongs to a class
Special method that sets up a new object
Protecting data and accessing it through methods

qs.q: Which best describes a class and an object?
c: A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it
An object is a blueprint; a class is one copy
A class is a type of loop
qs.e: Dog is the class. rex is an object (an instance) of Dog.

qs.q: Which method runs automatically when an object is created?
qs.e: The constructor sets up the new object's starting values.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
rex = Dog("Rex")
rex.learn()
rex.learn()
print(rex.tricks)

qs.e: tricks starts at 0 and learn() adds 1 twice.

q.py: What does self refer to inside a method?
q.java: What does this refer to inside a method?

qs.e: It refers to the specific object the method was called on.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
a = Dog("A")
b = Dog("B")
a.learn()
print(b.tricks)

qs.e: Each object has its own attributes. Teaching a doesn't change b.

qs.q: Keeping an object's data protected and changing it only through methods is called:
qs.e: Encapsulation hides data behind methods like getters and setters.

qs.q: How do you create a new Dog object named Rex?

e.py: Call the class like a function: Dog("Rex").
e.java: Use new followed by the constructor: new Dog("Rex").

UNITS.title: Debugging, Testing & Ethics
UNITS.blurb: Fix errors, test well, and be a good digital citizen.

list: <mark>Syntax error</mark>: breaks the language's grammar (missing colon, semicolon, or parenthesis). The program won't run at all.
<mark>Runtime error</mark>: the program starts but crashes, like dividing by zero or an index out of range.
<mark>Logic error</mark>: the program runs, but the answer is wrong. These are the hardest to find.
lesson.p: Every programmer makes errors. Knowing which kind you have tells you how to find it.

list: Read the error message. It usually names the line.
Trace the code by hand with a <mark>trace table</mark> that lists each variable's value after each step.
Add print statements to see values while it runs.
Explain your code out loud, line by line ("rubber duck debugging").

lesson.p: Good <mark>test cases</mark> include normal values, edge values, and invalid values. If valid input is 1 to 100, test 50 (normal), 1 and 100 (edges), and 0 and 101 (just outside). Testing the edges is called <mark>boundary testing</mark>.

list: Copying someone else's code and turning it in as yours is <mark>plagiarism</mark>. Give credit, and follow the <mark>license</mark> on open-source code.
Copyright protects creative work, including code, images, and music.
Protect your privacy: don't share passwords, your address, or personal details online.
Use strong, unique passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.
Cyberbullying has real consequences. Treat people online the way you would in person.

terms: Code that breaks the language's rules and won't run
An error that crashes the program while it runs
The program runs but gives the wrong result
A table tracking each variable's value step by step
Testing values at and just past the edges of valid input
Presenting someone else's work as your own
Rules for how others may use, share, and change code
The record of everything you do and post online

q.py: You forget the colon after an if statement. What kind of error is this?
q.java: You forget a semicolon at the end of a line. What kind of error is this?

qs.e: Breaking the language's grammar is a syntax error. The program won't run.

qs.q: A program crashes when the user enters 0 and the code divides by it. What kind of error is this?
qs.e: It starts fine and crashes while running, so it's a runtime error.

qs.q: A program averages 3 tests but divides the total by 2. It runs fine but gives the wrong answer. What kind of error is this?
qs.e: It runs but the result is wrong, so it's a logic error.

qs.q: Valid input is 1 to 100. Which set of tests is BEST for boundary testing?
qs.e: Test right at each edge and just past it.

qs.q: Your friend sends you their finished program, and you change the variable names and turn it in. This is:
qs.e: Renaming variables doesn't make the work yours.

qs.q: Which password is strongest?
qs.e: Long, mixed characters, and not personal or common.

qs.q: You want to use open-source code in your project. What should you do?
c: Use it and remove the author's name
Follow its license and give credit
Only use it if nobody will notice
You can't ever use other people's code
qs.e: Open-source licenses say how you may reuse the code, and they usually require credit.

qs.q: What is a trace table used for?
c: Tracking each variable's value as the code runs, step by step
qs.e: Trace tables help you find logic errors by following the code by hand.

qs.q: Which is the safest thing to post on a public profile?
qs.e: Location, schedules, and contact info can put your safety and privacy at risk.

UNITS.title: Hardware & Programming Languages
UNITS.blurb: CPU, memory, compilers vs. interpreters, and the limits of numbers.

lesson.p: The <mark>CPU</mark> (central processing unit) runs instructions. <mark>Primary memory</mark> (RAM) holds the program and data while it runs and is erased when power is off. <mark>Secondary storage</mark> (SSD, hard drive, flash drive) keeps files when the power is off. <mark>Peripherals</mark> are input and output devices like the keyboard, mouse, monitor, and printer.
People write code in high-level languages such as Python and Java. The computer only runs <mark>machine code</mark> (binary instructions), so the code must be translated.
list: A <mark>compiler</mark> translates the whole program before it runs. Java is compiled to bytecode, which the Java Virtual Machine runs.
An <mark>interpreter</mark> translates and runs the program line by line. Python is usually run by an interpreter.
Compiled programs catch many errors before running. Interpreted programs are quick to test and change.

lesson.p: In a <mark>strongly, statically typed</mark> language like Java, every variable has a declared type that cannot change. In a <mark>dynamically typed</mark> language like Python, a variable's type comes from the value stored in it and can change.

code.py:
x = 5        # x holds an int
x = "five"   # now x holds a str. Python allows this
code.java:
int x = 5;
x = "five";  // compile error: incompatible types

lesson.p: A <mark>local variable</mark> is created inside a function and exists only there. A <mark>global variable</mark> is created outside all functions and can be read anywhere in the file. Prefer local variables and parameters, because globals make bugs harder to find.

code.py:
count = 0          # global

def show():
    msg = "hi"     # local to show()
    print(msg, count)

p.py: Python integers can grow as large as memory allows, but decimals (floats) are stored in binary and can't be exact. 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004.
p.java: A Java int is 32 bits, so its largest value is 2,147,483,647. Adding 1 wraps around to -2,147,483,648. This is integer overflow. Doubles are stored in binary and can't be exact: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004.

code.java:
int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE;   // 2147483647
System.out.println(big + 1);   // -2147483648 (wraparound)
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2); // 0.30000000000000004

lesson.after: Never compare decimals with == when exact money or measurements matter. Round, or check whether the difference is very small.

lesson.p: A primitive variable stores a simple value directly, like a whole number or true/false. An object variable refers to a bundle of data and methods, like a String or a list. In Java, int, double, and boolean are primitives while String is an object. In Python, every value is an object.

terms: The processor that carries out program instructions
Fast, temporary memory that holds running programs and data
Long-term storage that keeps files with the power off
An input or output device connected to the computer
Translates a whole program before it runs
Translates and runs a program one line at a time
When a number is too big for its type and wraps around
A variable declared outside every function

qs.q: Which component carries out a program's instructions?
qs.e: The CPU (central processing unit) executes instructions.

qs.q: You save an essay and turn the computer off. Where does the file stay?
qs.e: RAM is erased without power. Secondary storage keeps files.

qs.q: Which device is a peripheral?
qs.e: Peripherals are input/output devices outside the core system, like printers and mice.

qs.q: What does an interpreter do?
c: Translates the whole program before running it
Translates and runs the program line by line
qs.e: An interpreter works line by line. A compiler translates the whole program first.

q.py: In Python, x = 5 and then x = "five" is allowed. Why?
q.java: In Java, int x = 5; x = "five"; causes an error. Why?

py: Strings and ints are the same

e.py: In a dynamically typed language, a variable takes the type of whatever value it holds.
e.java: A Java variable's declared type can't change, so an int variable can't hold a String.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.java: System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);

qs.e: Decimals are stored in binary and aren't exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004.

q.py: Which is true about integers in Python?

py: They can grow as large as memory allows

e.py: Python ints have no fixed size, so they don't wrap around.
e.java: A 32-bit int wraps around from the largest value to the smallest. That's integer overflow.

qs.q: A variable created inside a function is called:
qs.e: Local variables exist only inside the function where they're created.

UNITS.title: Style, Output & Graphics
UNITS.blurb: Readable code, clear prompts, formatted output, and simple drawings.

lesson.p: Programs are read by people far more often than they're written. Good <mark>programming style</mark> makes code easier to read, fix, and grade.
list: Use descriptive identifiers: total_price or totalPrice, not tp.
Add <mark>comments</mark> to explain why, not what every line does.
Use consistent <mark>indentation</mark> and white space between sections.
Follow your language's standard style (PEP 8 for Python, Java conventions for Java).

lesson.p: When a program asks for input, the prompt should tell the user exactly what to type. Output should be labeled so the user knows what each number means.

code.py:
# Ask clearly, label the result
name = input("Enter your first name: ")
age = int(input("Enter your age in years: "))
print("Name:", name)
print("Age next year:", age + 1)

lesson.p: Money and measurements should show a fixed number of decimal places, and tables should line up in columns.

code.py:
price = 4.5
print(f"Total: ${price:.2f}")       # Total: $4.50
print(f"{'Item':<8}{'Cost':>8}")
print(f"{'Taco':<8}{3.25:>8.2f}")

after.py: Inside an f-string, :.2f means two decimal places, < means left-align, and > means right-align.
after.java: In printf, %.2f means two decimal places, %-8s left-aligns in 8 spaces, and %n starts a new line.

lesson.p: <mark>Vector graphics</mark> are drawn from shapes defined by coordinates, like lines, circles, and rectangles, instead of a grid of pixels.

code.py:
import turtle
t = turtle.Turtle()

t.forward(100)          # a line 100 pixels long
t.circle(50)            # a circle with radius 50
for side in range(4):   # a 100 x 60 rectangle
    t.forward(100 if side % 2 == 0 else 60)
    t.left(90)
turtle.done()

after.py: In turtle, forward moves and draws, left turns in degrees, and circle draws using a radius.
after.java: drawOval takes x, y, width, height. When width equals height, you get a circle.

terms: The name you give a variable, function, or class
A note in code that the computer ignores
Spacing at the start of a line that shows code structure
Text that tells the user what to enter
Output with set decimal places, widths, and alignment
Images drawn from shapes defined by coordinates
A shared set of rules for writing readable code

qs.q: Which variable name follows good style?
qs.e: Descriptive identifiers say what the value means.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of a comment?
c: Explain the code to people reading it
qs.e: Comments are ignored by the computer and help human readers.

qs.q: Which prompt is clearest?
qs.e: A good prompt says exactly what to type, including the allowed range.

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py:
price = 7.5
print(f"${price:.2f}")
code.java:
double price = 7.5;
System.out.printf("$%.2f%n", price);

qs.e: .2f shows exactly two digits after the decimal point.

qs.q: Why is the second print better?

code.py:
print(42)
print("Average score:", 42)
code.java:
System.out.println(42);
System.out.println("Average score: " + 42);

c: The output is labeled so the user knows what 42 means
qs.e: Labeled output tells the user what each value represents.

q.py: In turtle, what does t.circle(50) draw?

e.py: turtle.circle takes a radius.
e.java: When width and height are equal, drawOval draws a circle.

qs.q: Which is a vector graphic shape?
qs.e: Vector graphics are built from shapes like lines, circles, and rectangles.

qs.q: Consistent indentation mainly helps with:
qs.e: Indentation shows which lines belong together. In Python, it's also required by the language.

UNITS.title: Math, Random & Error Handling
UNITS.blurb: Math functions, random numbers, classic algorithms, and safe programs.

lesson.p: Languages include ready-made math functions so you don't have to write them yourself.

code.py:
import math
print(abs(-7))          # 7
print(round(3.14159, 2)) # 3.14
print(2 ** 5)           # 32 (power)
print(math.sqrt(49))    # 7.0
print(6 ** 2)           # 36 (square)
code.java:
System.out.println(Math.abs(-7));       // 7
System.out.println(Math.round(3.6));    // 4
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 5));     // 32.0
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(49));      // 7.0
System.out.println(6 * 6);              // 36 (square)

lesson.p: Games, simulations, and quizzes use <mark>random numbers</mark>.

code.py:
import random
die = random.randint(1, 6)    # 1 to 6, both included
coin = random.choice(["H", "T"])
print(die, coin)

after.py: random.randint(a, b) includes both a and b.
after.java: nextInt(6) gives 0 through 5, so add 1 for a die roll.

lesson.p: These algorithms show up again and again in CS I.
list: <mark>Largest of three</mark>: compare a to b, then the winner to c.
<mark>Average</mark>: add the values with an accumulator, then divide by the count.
<mark>Prime check</mark>: a number n > 1 is prime if no number from 2 up to the square root of n divides it evenly.
<mark>GCD</mark> (Euclid): replace (a, b) with (b, a % b) until b is 0. Then a is the GCD.
<mark>Making change</mark>: use integer division and % to count quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies.

code.py:
def gcd(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

print(gcd(48, 18))   # 6

cents = 68
quarters = cents // 25   # 2
cents = cents % 25       # 18 left

lesson.p: Programs should not crash on bad input. Use <mark>exception handling</mark> to catch common errors like <mark>division by zero</mark> and <mark>type mismatch</mark> (letters typed where a number was expected).

list: <mark>Lexical error</mark>: a character or token the language doesn't recognize, such as an unclosed string.
<mark>Syntax error</mark>: the words are real, but the grammar is wrong, such as a missing colon or semicolon.
<mark>Run-time error</mark>: the program crashes while running, such as dividing by zero.
<mark>Logic error</mark>: the program runs but gives the wrong answer.

terms: Built-in functions like abs, round, pow, and sqrt
An unpredictable value a program generates
Greatest common divisor: the largest number that divides both values
A whole number above 1 divisible only by 1 and itself
An error event that happens while a program runs
Code that catches errors so the program doesn't crash
A character or token the language doesn't recognize

qs.q: What is printed?

code.py: print(abs(-12) + 3)
code.java: System.out.println(Math.abs(-12) + 3);

e.py: randint includes both ends, so 1 through 6.
e.java: nextInt(6) gives 0-5. Adding 1 gives 1-6.

qs.q: What is the GCD of 48 and 18?
How many quarters are in 68 cents?

code.java: System.out.println(68 / 25);

qs.e: Integer division drops the remainder: 68 divided by 25 is 2 whole quarters.

qs.q: Which number is prime?
qs.e: 29 has no divisors besides 1 and 29. 21 = 3×7, 27 = 3×9, 33 = 3×11.

qs.q: A user types "ten" when the program expects a number. What kind of problem is this?
c: A lexical error in the code
qs.e: Text was entered where a number was expected. Handle it with try/except or try/catch.

qs.q: Which error makes a program run but give the wrong answer?
qs.e: Logic errors don't crash the program. They produce wrong results.

q.py: Which exception does 10 / 0 raise in Python?
q.java: Which exception does 10 / 0 (int division) throw in Java?

e.py: Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError.
e.java: Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

qs.q: Which algorithm finds the largest of three numbers a, b, c?
c: Compare a and b, then compare the larger one to c
qs.e: Two comparisons are enough: find the larger of a and b, then compare it to c.

UNITS.title: Digital Citizenship & Security
UNITS.blurb: Copyright, licenses, privacy, safe passwords, and tech's impact.

lesson.p: <mark>Intellectual property</mark> is creative work that belongs to someone, including code, music, images, and writing. <mark>Copyright</mark> protects it automatically when it's created.
list: <mark>Proprietary</mark> software: you buy a license to use it, but can't copy or change it.
<mark>Open-source</mark> software: the code is shared, and its license says how you may use, change, and share it.
<mark>Public domain</mark>: no copyright restrictions remain.
Always credit sources and follow the license, even for free code you find online.

lesson.p: Schools and employers have an <mark>acceptable use policy</mark> (AUP) that explains how their devices and networks may be used. <mark>Digital etiquette</mark> means being respectful online: no harassment, no spam, and no sharing other people's information without permission.

list: Use long <mark>passphrases</mark> like four random words with a number and symbol.
Never reuse one password across many sites.
Turn on <mark>two-factor authentication</mark> (2FA), which asks for a second proof like a code on your phone.
Watch for <mark>phishing</mark>: messages that pretend to be trusted senders to steal logins.

lesson.p: <mark>Malware</mark> is software designed to cause harm, including viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware. Prevent it by keeping software updated, using antivirus protection, downloading only from trusted sources, and not opening unexpected attachments.
Apps collect data about what you do. Read privacy settings, share less personal information, and think before posting. Anything posted online can be copied and stay public.

New technology like <mark>artificial intelligence</mark>, facial recognition, and self-driving cars brings benefits and risks. Ask: Who benefits? Who could be harmed? Is the data fair and private? Is it used ethically?

terms: Creative work that legally belongs to its creator
Legal protection for original creative work
Rules for how software may be used, changed, and shared
Software whose code is shared under a license
Rules for using an organization's devices and network
Logging in with a password plus a second proof
Software designed to harm a computer or steal data
A fake message that tricks people into revealing information

qs.q: You find code on a website with an open-source license. What should you do?
c: Follow the license and credit the author
qs.e: Open-source licenses allow use under specific conditions, which usually include giving credit.

qs.q: Which password is strongest?
qs.e: Long passphrases with mixed characters are much harder to guess.

qs.q: What is two-factor authentication?
c: A password plus a second proof like a phone code
Sharing your password with a friend
qs.e: 2FA adds a second factor, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

qs.q: An email says it's from your school and asks for your password at a link. This is:
qs.e: Phishing fakes a trusted sender to steal credentials.

qs.q: What is an acceptable use policy?
c: Rules for using an organization's computers and network
qs.e: An AUP explains what you may and may not do on school or work technology.

qs.q: Which action best prevents malware?
c: Downloading only from trusted sources and keeping software updated
qs.e: Updates close security holes, and trusted sources reduce risk.

qs.q: Copyright protects a song you wrote:
c: Automatically, as soon as it's created
qs.e: In the U.S., copyright applies automatically once a work is created in fixed form.

qs.q: A city wants to use facial recognition in schools. Which is an ethical question to ask?
c: Is the data private and is the system fair to everyone?
Which font does the app use?
qs.e: Ethical review asks who benefits, who could be harmed, and whether data is fair and private.

UNITS.title: Careers & Teamwork in CS
UNITS.blurb: Jobs, college programs, portfolios, and working on a team.

lesson.p: Computer science skills are used in almost every industry, including healthcare, energy, games, finance, and government.
list: <mark>Software developer</mark>: designs and builds apps and systems.
<mark>Web developer</mark>: builds websites and web apps.
<mark>Data analyst / data scientist</mark>: finds patterns in data.
<mark>Cybersecurity analyst</mark>: protects systems and networks.
<mark>Product or project manager</mark>: plans what gets built and keeps teams on track.
<mark>Game developer</mark>, <mark>IT support specialist</mark>, and <mark>AI/machine learning engineer</mark>.
<mark>Internships</mark> give real work experience while you're still in school.
A <mark>resume</mark> is a one-page summary of your skills, experience, and education.
A <mark>portfolio</mark> shows your best projects, often on GitHub or a personal website.
<mark>Certifications</mark> (such as industry IT, cloud, or programming certificates) prove specific skills.
Compare <mark>university programs</mark> by courses offered, cost, internships, and outcomes like graduation and job placement.

lesson.p: Most software is built by teams. Good teammates communicate clearly, share the work, meet deadlines, and accept feedback.
list: <mark>Technical writing</mark>: clear documentation, comments, and README files.
<mark>Code review</mark>: teammates check each other's code and suggest fixes.
Plan your time: break work into tasks and set deadlines.
Be a leader and a learner: help others, ask questions, and respond well to feedback.

lesson.p: Professionals protect user data, respect copyright and licenses, test their work, and are honest about what their software can and can't do.

terms: Short-term, real work experience while studying
A one-page summary of skills, experience, and education
A collection of your best projects to show employers
A credential that proves a specific skill
Clear documentation that explains how something works
A person who designs and builds software

qs.q: Which best shows an employer what you can build?
qs.e: A portfolio, such as a GitHub profile or website, shows real work.

qs.q: Who protects systems and networks from attacks?
qs.e: Cybersecurity analysts defend systems and respond to threats.

qs.q: What is an internship?
c: Short-term work experience while you're studying
qs.e: Internships give real-world experience and connections.

qs.q: A teammate suggests a fix in a code review. The best response is to:
c: Consider it, ask questions, and apply it if it improves the code
qs.e: Seeking and responding to feedback improves the quality of your product.

qs.q: Which is the best example of technical writing?
c: A text message to a friend
A README that explains how to install and run a program
qs.e: Technical writing explains how something works clearly and accurately.

qs.q: When comparing university computer science programs, which factor matters?
c: The color of the campus buildings
Courses offered, cost, and internship opportunities
How many vending machines there are
qs.e: Courses, cost, internships, and outcomes help you choose a program.

qs.q: Your team has a project due in two weeks. What's the best plan?
c: Break it into tasks with owners and deadlines
qs.e: Planning and time management keep teams on schedule.

qs.q: A resume should usually be:
c: A clear, one-page summary of skills, experience, and education
qs.e: Early-career resumes are typically one page and easy to scan.
